chapter.name: Oscillations
chapter.blurb: The chapter introduces periodic and oscillatory motion and the ideas of period, frequency and displacement, and defines simple harmonic motion by x = A cos(omega t + phi). It connects SHM with uniform circular motion, obtains the velocity, acceleration, force law and energy of a simple harmonic oscillator, and applies them to a block on a spring. It ends by showing that a simple pendulum swinging through small angles is simple harmonic with period 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

scope_in.item: Distinguish periodic motion from oscillatory motion, describe the equilibrium position and the force that brings a displaced body back, and give examples (every oscillatory motion is periodic, not every periodic motion is oscillatory)
Define period and frequency, use nu = 1/T and the hertz, and calculate one from the other or from a count of oscillations in a given time (Example 13.1)

Use 'displacement' in the general sense of any property that varies with time, and recognise periodic and non-periodic functions of time, with the period 2 pi/omega of sine and cosine functions and of their combinations (Eqs. 13.3a-d, Example 13.2)

State the displacement equation x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi) of SHM and identify amplitude, phase, phase constant and angular frequency; use omega = 2 pi/T = 2 pi nu and read these quantities from a given equation (Example 13.3)

Describe SHM as the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter (reference particle and reference circle) and write the SHM of the x-projection from the radius, period, initial position and sense of revolution (Example 13.4, Exercises 13.11-13.12)

Use v(t) = -omega A sin(omega t + phi) and a(t) = -omega^2 A cos(omega t + phi) = -omega^2 x, the velocity and acceleration amplitudes omega A and omega^2 A, the signs of v and a at different points, and their phase differences pi/2 and pi with the displacement (Example 13.5, Exercises 13.5, 13.6, 13.14)

State the force law F = -kx with k = m omega^2, omega = sqrt(k/m) and T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); explain restoring force and linear and non-linear oscillators; apply these to a block on a horizontal spring and to a block between two identical springs (Example 13.6, Exercise 13.9)

Calculate the kinetic energy, the potential energy U = (1/2) k x^2 and the total energy E = (1/2) k A^2 of a simple harmonic oscillator, and explain their variation with time and displacement, their period T/2 and the conservation of the total (Example 13.7)

Describe the forces and the restoring torque on a simple pendulum, use the small-angle approximation sin(theta) = theta (Table 13.1) to show the motion is SHM, and use T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), including the pendulum that ticks seconds and a change of g (Example 13.8, Exercise 13.15)

concepts.name: Periodic and oscillatory motion: period, frequency, displacement and periodic functions
concepts.description: What periodic and oscillatory motions are, the period and frequency of a periodic motion, displacement as a general variable, and sine and cosine functions of time as periodic functions.
concepts.idea: A motion that repeats itself at regular intervals of time is periodic; if the body also moves to and fro about a mean (equilibrium) position the motion is oscillatory, and it is described by a displacement that is a periodic function of time.
concepts.rule: The smallest interval of time after which a periodic motion repeats is its period T (SI unit second). The number of repetitions per unit time is the frequency nu = 1/T, measured in hertz (1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second = 1 s^-1); nu need not be an integer. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but every periodic motion need not be oscillatory (uniform circular motion is periodic, not oscillatory). At the equilibrium position no net external force acts; a small displacement brings into play a force that tries to bring the body back. Displacement here means the change with time of any physical property (position, angle of a pendulum, voltage across a capacitor) and may be positive or negative. f(t) = A cos omega t and A sin omega t are periodic with period T = 2 pi/omega; A sin omega t + B cos omega t = D sin(omega t + phi) with D = sqrt(A^2 + B^2) and tan phi = B/A has the same period. A sum of such terms repeats after the least time that is a whole multiple of every term's period; e^(-omega t) and log(omega t) never repeat and are not periodic.
concepts.example: A child on a swing completes 30 oscillations in 60 s: frequency nu = 30/60 = 0.5 Hz and period T = 1/nu = 2 s.

concepts.name: Simple harmonic motion: the displacement equation, amplitude, phase and angular frequency
concepts.description: Simple harmonic motion defined by x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi); the meaning of amplitude, phase, phase constant and angular frequency, and how omega is related to the period and the frequency.
concepts.idea: Simple harmonic motion is not just any periodic motion: it is the oscillation in which the displacement from the origin is a sinusoidal function of time, fixed by three constants A, omega and phi.
concepts.rule: x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi). A is the amplitude, the magnitude of the maximum displacement, so x varies between +A and -A. The time-dependent quantity (omega t + phi) is the phase; its value at t = 0 is the phase constant (phase angle) phi, which, if the amplitude is known, can be found from the displacement at t = 0. omega is the angular frequency, SI unit radian per second, with omega = 2 pi/T = 2 pi nu. Two SHMs may differ only in amplitude, only in phase constant, or only in angular frequency. The period stays fixed whatever location is chosen as the initial one. A combination such as sin omega t - cos omega t = sqrt(2) sin(omega t - pi/4) is again an SHM of period 2 pi/omega; sin^2 omega t = 1/2 - (1/2) cos 2 omega t repeats with period pi/omega.
concepts.example: x = 0.2 cos(10 pi t + pi/6), with x in m and t in s: amplitude 0.2 m, angular frequency 10 pi rad/s, period T = 2 pi/(10 pi) = 0.2 s, frequency 5 Hz, phase constant pi/6.

questions.a: omega = 2 pi/T = 2 pi/0.25 = 8 pi rad/s. So x = 4 cos(8 pi t + pi/6), x in cm, t in s. Phase at t = 1 s = omega t + phi = 8 pi + pi/6 = 49 pi/6 rad.

Phase at t = 1 s = 8 pi + pi/6 = 49 pi/6 rad

questions.q: A displacement is given by x(t) = sqrt(3) sin omega t + cos omega t, where omega is a positive constant. Show that it can be written as x = A cos(omega t + phi), find A and phi, and state the period. (cos(pi/3) = 1/2, sin(pi/3) = sqrt(3)/2.)
questions.a: Expand A cos(omega t + phi) = A cos phi cos omega t - A sin phi sin omega t. Comparing with cos omega t + sqrt(3) sin omega t: A cos phi = 1 and -A sin phi = sqrt(3). Squaring and adding, A^2 = 1 + 3 = 4, so A = 2. Then cos phi = 1/2 and sin phi = -sqrt(3)/2, so phi = -pi/3 (equivalently 5 pi/3). Hence x = 2 cos(omega t - pi/3), a simple harmonic motion of amplitude 2 and period T = 2 pi/omega.
s: Matches coefficients (A cos phi = 1, A sin phi = -sqrt(3)) or an equivalent correct method
phi = -pi/3 (or 5 pi/3), so x = 2 cos(omega t - pi/3), with period 2 pi/omega

questions.q: A student claims: 'sin^2 omega t has the same period, 2 pi/omega, as sin omega t.' Using sin^2 omega t = 1/2 - (1/2) cos 2 omega t, evaluate the claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. The only time-dependent part is cos 2 omega t, whose angular frequency is 2 omega, so it repeats after 2 pi/(2 omega) = pi/omega. concepts.name: Simple harmonic motion and uniform circular motion
concepts.description: The projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter of the circle as simple harmonic motion: the reference particle and reference circle, and writing the SHM of the x-projection from the radius, period, initial position and sense of revolution.
concepts.idea: If a particle P moves uniformly on a circle, its projection P' on a diameter of the circle moves to and fro in simple harmonic motion.
concepts.rule: Let P move anticlockwise on a circle of radius A with angular speed omega, its position vector OP making an angle phi with the positive x-axis at t = 0. After time t, OP makes an angle (omega t + phi), so the projection on the x-axis is x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi), the defining equation of SHM. P is the reference particle and its circle the reference circle. The radius is the amplitude, the angular speed is the angular frequency (omega = 2 pi/T, with T the period of revolution) and the initial angle is the phase constant. The projection on the y-axis, y = A sin(omega t + phi), is an SHM of the same amplitude differing in phase by pi/2. For clockwise revolution the angle decreases with time: starting from pi/2 it is (pi/2 - 2 pi t/T). In spite of this connection, the force on a particle in linear SHM is very different from the centripetal force needed for uniform circular motion.
concepts.example: A particle goes anticlockwise round a circle of radius 3 cm once in 10 s, starting on the positive x-axis: omega = 2 pi/10 = pi/5 rad/s, so its x-projection is x = 3 cos(pi t/5), with x in cm and t in s.

concepts.name: Velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion
concepts.description: The velocity and acceleration of a particle in SHM as functions of time, their maximum values, the relation a = -omega^2 x, and their phase relations with the displacement.
concepts.idea: In SHM the velocity and the acceleration also vary sinusoidally with the same period as the displacement, but out of step with it: the acceleration is always proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position.
concepts.rule: For x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi): v(t) = dx/dt = -omega A sin(omega t + phi) and a(t) = dv/dt = -omega^2 A cos(omega t + phi) = -omega^2 x(t). The velocity amplitude is v_m = omega A and the acceleration amplitude is a_m = omega^2 A, so v varies from -omega A to +omega A and a from -omega^2 A to +omega^2 A. For x > 0, a < 0 and for x < 0, a > 0: the acceleration is always directed towards the centre. The speed is maximum at x = 0 and zero at the extremes; the acceleration is zero at x = 0 and greatest in magnitude at the extremes. All three quantities have the same period T; relative to the displacement, the velocity has a phase difference of pi/2 (velocity leads displacement by pi/2) and the acceleration a phase difference of pi (opposite in phase). A relation between a and x describes SHM only if it has the form a = -(positive constant) x.
concepts.example: x = 2 cos(5t), with x in cm and t in s: v_m = omega A = 5 x 2 = 10 cm/s and a_m = omega^2 A = 25 x 2 = 50 cm/s^2; when x = 1 cm, a = -omega^2 x = -25 cm/s^2.

concepts.name: Force law for simple harmonic motion and the block-spring oscillator
concepts.description: The restoring force F = -kx, the relations k = m omega^2 and omega = sqrt(k/m), the period of a block on a spring, the linear harmonic oscillator, and the block held between two identical springs.
concepts.idea: A particle executes SHM whenever the force on it is proportional to its displacement and always directed towards the mean position; the constant of proportionality and the mass together fix how fast it oscillates.
concepts.rule: From F = ma and a = -omega^2 x, the force on a particle of mass m in SHM is F(t) = -m omega^2 x(t) = -k x(t), with k = m omega^2, so omega = sqrt(k/m) and T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k). The force is always directed towards the mean position and is called the restoring force. SHM can be defined equivalently by x = A cos(omega t + phi) or by the force law F = -kx: differentiating the displacement twice gives the force law, and integrating the force law twice gives back the displacement. A particle oscillating under a force linearly proportional to x is a linear harmonic oscillator; if the force has small extra terms in x^2, x^3 it is a non-linear oscillator. A block on a frictionless horizontal surface attached to a spring of spring constant k obeys F = -kx, with x measured from the equilibrium position. For a block between two identical springs fixed to supports, a displacement x stretches one spring and compresses the other, each giving -kx, so F = -2kx and T = 2 pi sqrt(m/2k).
concepts.example: A block of mass 0.2 kg on a frictionless horizontal surface is attached to a spring of spring constant 180 N/m: omega = sqrt(180/0.2) = 30 rad/s and T = 2 pi/30 = 0.209 s (pi = 3.14).

concepts.name: Energy in simple harmonic motion
concepts.description: The kinetic, potential and total mechanical energies of a particle in SHM as functions of time and of displacement, and the conservation of the total energy.
concepts.idea: In SHM the energy keeps changing form between kinetic and potential, each varying between zero and a maximum, while their sum stays constant.
concepts.rule: Kinetic energy K = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) k A^2 sin^2(omega t + phi): zero at the extremes and maximum at the mean position. Potential energy of the conservative force F = -kx is U = (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2) k A^2 cos^2(omega t + phi): zero at the mean position and maximum at the extremes. Total energy E = K + U = (1/2) k A^2, independent of time, as expected for a conservative force when no friction is present. Hence at displacement x, K = E - U = (1/2) k (A^2 - x^2). K and U are never negative, each repeats with period T/2 and each peaks twice in every period of the motion; between x = 0 (all kinetic) and x = +A or -A (all potential), one increases at the expense of the other.
concepts.example: A spring-block oscillator with k = 200 N/m and amplitude 0.2 m has total energy E = (1/2)(200)(0.2)^2 = 4 J; at x = 0.16 m the potential energy is (1/2)(200)(0.16)^2 = 2.56 J and the kinetic energy is 4 - 2.56 = 1.44 J.

concepts.name: The simple pendulum
concepts.description: The forces and restoring torque on the bob of a simple pendulum, the small-angle approximation that makes its motion simple harmonic, and the period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
concepts.idea: A small bob on a light inextensible string swings in very nearly simple harmonic motion when the angle of swing is small, with a period fixed only by the length of the string and the acceleration due to gravity.
concepts.rule: A simple pendulum is a small bob of mass m tied to an inextensible massless string of length L fixed to a rigid support; theta is the angle of the string with the vertical (theta = 0 at the mean position). Only two forces act on the bob: the tension T along the string and gravity mg. mg resolves into mg cos(theta) along the string and mg sin(theta) perpendicular to it. The net radial force T - mg cos(theta) gives the radial acceleration and no torque about the support; the tangential component gives the restoring torque tau = -L mg sin(theta), the negative sign showing that it tends to reduce theta. With tau = I alpha, alpha = -(mgL/I) sin(theta). For small theta in radians sin(theta) is nearly theta (even at 20 degrees: 0.349 rad against sin = 0.342), so alpha = -(mgL/I) theta, which has the same form as a = -omega^2 x: the motion is SHM with omega = sqrt(mgL/I) and T = 2 pi sqrt(I/mgL). The string is massless, so I = m L^2 and T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g). A pendulum that ticks seconds has T = 2 s and, for g = 9.8 m/s^2, length about 1 m.
concepts.example: A simple pendulum of length 2.5 m swinging through small angles where g = 10 m/s^2 has T = 2 pi sqrt(2.5/10) = 2 pi x 0.5 = pi s, about 3.14 s.

Compares with a = -omega^2 x: SHM with omega = sqrt(m g L/I), T = 2 pi sqrt(I/(m g L))

questions.a: The statement is wrong. The restoring torque is proportional to sin(theta), not to theta. The period formula is obtained only after replacing sin(theta) by theta, which is a good approximation only for small angles (the book's table shows it holding up to about 20 degrees). For a large angle such as 60 degrees sin(theta) differs appreciably from theta in radians, so the angular acceleration is not proportional to the angular displacement and the motion is not simple harmonic.
s: Judgement - incorrect: the formula rests on the approximation sin(theta) = theta, valid only for small angles
For large angles the restoring torque (proportional to sin(theta)) is not proportional to theta, so the motion is not SHM

State its length, say what you would choose for the bob's mass and the angle of swing and why, and predict the period of your pendulum at a place where g = 2.5 m/s^2.
questions.a: L = g T^2/(4 pi^2) = (10 x 9)/(4 x 10) = 2.25 m. Any small bob will do (for example 0.1 kg), since the period does not depend on the mass; the angle of swing should be kept small (well within about 20 degrees) so that sin(theta) is nearly theta and the motion is simple harmonic. Where g = 2.5 m/s^2, g is one-quarter as large, so T is sqrt(4) = 2 times as long: T = 6 s (check: 2 pi sqrt(2.25/2.5) = 2 pi x 0.949 = 6 s with pi^2 = 10).
s: Length L = g T^2/(4 pi^2) = 2.25 m
Any bob mass (period independent of mass) and a small angle of swing so that the motion is SHM
Period where g = 2.5 m/s^2 is 6 s, by any correct method
